claims.text: TypeSafe AI opened early access to Jev, their SystemOne model, in the week before this post (September 2026).
Jev is TypeSafe AI's SystemOne model.
TypeSafe's Jev provides a set of AI primitives that let apps, agents, and workflows make decisions based on context.
Jev's decision-making primitives are confidence scoring, multiple choice, and yes/no (noul) questions.
Jev's decision-making primitives are the perfect complement to agentic work.
Combining Jev's reasoning with Pulumi makes the gap between designing infrastructure and deploying it to production practically vanish.
Having more choices in the past usually meant more complexity and technical debt.
GeoDeploy compares every AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud region that offers managed Kubernetes and picks the best one for each geo.

A GeoDeploy deployment request has four parts: target geos (traffic share and data-residency rule: EU-only, US-only, or in-country), an image with platforms (amd64, arm64, or both), a workload shape (replicas, CPU and memory per pod, egress, storage), and constraints (allowed providers, max provider count, budget).
GeoDeploy provisions consistent environments across AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud.

In GeoDeploy, the TypeScript app takes in the request, fetches live pricing and does all the math but never makes judgment calls; Jev decides region and modules but never does arithmetic, generates code, or invents region names; Pulumi provisions clusters, registries, workloads, and DNS but decides nothing.
GeoDeploy lists every region with managed Kubernetes and uses great-circle distance as a coverage measure.
GeoDeploy gets current prices from the AWS Price List API, the Azure Retail Prices API, and the Google Cloud Billing Catalog.
GeoDeploy's deterministic TypeScript bin-packs pods onto nodes, filters out instance types that don't match the image's architecture, and computes a monthly cost per candidate.
GeoDeploy composes a Pulumi program from a registry of typed modules: EKS, AKS, or GKE; ECR, ACR, or Artifact Registry; ingress; DNS through Route 53, NS1, or Cloudflare; and observability.
GeoDeploy uses the Pulumi Automation API to run a preview and then an update, with one stack per region.
GeoDeploy will not run provisioning unless cloud credentials pass readiness checks.
Every GeoDeploy run writes plan.json and plan.md with the full decision record, and a web UI shows the deployment on a live globe.
Jev doesn't return free text; it returns typed answers with calibrated confidence through three primitives.
Jev's `choice()` primitive picks one option from a closed list and returns the pick, a probability distribution across all options, and a confidence.
Jev's `score()` primitive rates something against a rubric you describe; GeoDeploy uses 10 levels.
Jev's `noul()` primitive answers a yes/no question with a single probability.
Jev only selects from closed sets, never writes code or does arithmetic, so a hallucinated region or made-up Pulumi argument can't happen by construction.
For each geo, GeoDeploy sends Jev a shortlist of up to 40 priced candidates with constraints and the image's architecture, in a single call.

GeoDeploy asks Jev for a region selection (choice), five quality scores (coverage, cost fit, maturity, sprawl risk, architecture consistency), two hard checks (data residency and capacity via noul), and a fallback region (choice).
packages/decide/src/questions.ts in the devx-geodeploy repo contains buildStageAQuestions, importing choice, noul, score from "@typesafe-ai/sdk".
TypeSafe advises to "describe situations, not degrees" when writing rubrics.

GeoDeploy's rubrics have 10 levels each, running from "Serves users on a different continent with no nearby presence" to "In-geo with multiple availability zones, directly in or adjacent to the demand geo's primary population center."

The TypeSafe SDK provides a TypeSafeClient with a systemOne method taking state and questions and returning answers with fields such as selection.choice, selection.confidence, residencyOk.noul, coverage.score.
GeoDeploy's ranking uses weight profiles: latency-optimized (default), balanced, residency-first, and failure-domain; weights live in code so ranking can be re-tuned without calling Jev again.

GeoDeploy weight profiles: latency-optimized cost 0.13, coverage 0.48, maturity 0.17, sprawl 0.1, archConsistency 0.12; balanced 0.25/0.25/0.2/0.12/0.18; residency-first 0.12/0.12/0.38/0.23/0.15; failure-domain 0.08/0.17/0.48/0.15/0.12.
Every extra cloud provider means more credentials, tooling, and on-call runbooks.
In GeoDeploy, cluster and registry modules follow from the provider (AWS means EKS and ECR), leaving Jev to decide ingress posture, autoscaling posture, and node-pool sizing tier.

GeoDeploy confidence thresholds: data residency 0.95 (hard reject); region for a new cluster 0.90 (top three candidates flagged for human choice); region when stack exists 0.75 (keep existing region); ingress or autoscaling module 0.85 (registry default); node-pool sizing tier 0.60 (bin-packing result); global floor for region pick, residency, or capacity 0.50 (drop the AI path for that geo).
The residency check lives in packages/decide/src/engine.ts in the devx-geodeploy repo.
Each AiPathAborted in GeoDeploy carries the full attempt (state, questions, answers), so rejected answers end up in the audit trail.

If a gate check fails, the API times out or errors, or the upstream can't be reached, GeoDeploy falls back to a deterministic mode comparing prices across providers while still enforcing residency and constraint checks.
The `geodeploy explain` command shows why each region won.

With self-driving mode enabled via `geodeploy monitor`, GeoDeploy periodically checks each deployment's CPU utilization and asks Jev one joint question across all regions with options no-change, scale-up:<geo>, scale-down:<geo>, or shift:<from>-><to>, plus a separate disruption-risk check; code computes node-count changes.

In self-driving mode, above 0.85 confidence the resize is applied automatically; between 0.70 and 0.85 it is suggested for human approval; below 0.70 GeoDeploy ignores Jev's pick and uses a deterministic per-region rule based on observed utilization.
CPU utilization alone makes a poor autoscaling metric and is usually paired with other signals such as median request latency and error rates.
GeoDeploy is released as open source at github.com/pulumi/devx-geodeploy.
The Pulumi Automation API page is at /automation/.
